abstract.text: Can any secrets still be shed by that much studied, uniquely integrable, Elliptic Billiard? Starting by examining the family of 3-periodic trajectories and the loci of their Triangular Centers, one obtains a beautiful and variegated gallery of curves: ellipses, quartics, sextics, circles, and even a stationary point. Secondly, one notices this family conserves an intriguing ratio: Inradius-to-Circumradius. In turn this implies three conservation corollaries: (i) the sum of bounce angle cosines, (ii) the product of excentral cosines, and (iii) the ratio of excentral-to-orbit areas. Monge’s Orthoptic Circle’s close relation to 4-periodic Billiard trajectories is well-known. Its geometry provided clues with which to generalize 3-periodic invariants to trajectories of an arbitrary number of edges. This was quite unexpected. Indeed, the Elliptic Billiard did surprise us!

source_span.start_text: Can the Elliptic Billiard Still Surprise Us?

sections.summary: The introduction frames the elliptic billiard as an exhaustively studied integrable system and asks whether it can still surprise. It recounts the authors’ earlier discovery that the 3-periodic Incenter locus is an ellipse, the subsequent proofs for several triangle centers, and the experimental approach through an interactive applet and locus gallery. Monge’s Orthoptic Circle is introduced as the bridge to generalizing invariants to N>3.
sections.title: Introduction: Why Revisit the Elliptic Billiard?

source_span.end_text: Let the boundary of the EB satisfy f (x, y) = (x/a)2 + (y/b)2 = 1, where (a, b) are the semi-axes.

sections.summary: Supplies geometric and dynamical background: definitions of triangle centers and derived triangles from Figure 3; the elliptic billiard as a 4D integrable Hamiltonian system with energy and Joachimsthal integrals; Poncelet’s Porism; and Monge’s Orthoptic Circle and its N=4 parallelogram orbits. It sets up vocabulary and classical facts used by the later conservation and locus arguments.
sections.title: Background: Triangle Centers, Integrability, Poncelet, and Monge

source_span.end_text: Every triangle has a circumellipse to which it is a Billiard orbit, whose center coincides with the triangle’s Mittenpunkt.
source_span.start_text: Consider an EB centered at O, and an N = 3 orbit, shown in Figure 6a.

sections.summary: Presents the N=3 locus gallery. Incenter, Barycenter, Circumcenter, Orthocenter, and 9-point center X5 produce ellipses; Excenters produce an ellipse similar to a rotated Incenter locus. Numerically only 29 of the first 100 Kimberling centers yield elliptic loci. Derived triangles generally produce non-elliptic loci, but Extouchpoints form an ellipse identical to the Caustic; Feuerbach Point X11 traces the Caustic while its anticomplement X100 traces the Billiard; Mittenpunkt X9 is stationary at the billiard center, implying every triangle has a Circumbilliard with center at its Mittenpunkt.
sections.title: N=3 Locus Gallery: Ellipses, Exceptions, and the Stationary Mittenpunkt

source_span.end_text: A 3-periodic family conserves the Excentral-to-Orbit area ratio.
source_span.start_text: In this Section we describe how we’ve stumbled upon an incredible manifestation

sections.summary: Derives the conserved Inradius-to-Circumradius ratio r/R for 3-periodic orbits, expressed as γL−4. Using classical triangle identities, it obtains three conservation corollaries: sum of orbit-angle cosines, product of excentral cosines, and excentral-to-orbit area ratio. It notes r/R is maximal at 0.5 for the circular billiard and tends to zero as a/b→∞.
sections.title: Conserved r/R Ratio and Its Triangle-Identity Corollaries

source_span.start_text: Loci can be ellipses, but can they be a circle?

sections.summary: Begins with the N=3 circular locus of Q1/Q2, centered on the billiard and with radius r*=r(L/4+1/γ), linked to the Excentral Triangle’s Cosine Circle. Then uses N=4/Monge clues to generalize invariants to N>3: stationary tangential-polygon point, generalized extouchpoints on the caustic, conservation of cosine sum and product for all N, odd-N area-ratio conservation, and circular loci for N>4, with a momentum-conservation proof giving radius 1/γ.
sections.title: Circular Loci and Generalizing Invariants to N>3

source_span.end_text: Postscript: Elegant proofs for some of the N > 3 invariants have recently appeared [2, 3].
source_span.start_text: The reader is invited to check out more details about this work on a companion website [21].

sections.summary: Concludes with open questions about algebraic/elliptic loci, 3D analogues, self-intersecting orbits, non-billiard Poncelet families, spherical/ellipsoidal billiards, and formulas for remaining constants. It also provides a quick-reference video table and notes a postscript on subsequent proofs for some N>3 invariants.
sections.title: Conclusion, Open Questions, and Video Reference

question.text: Can the elliptic billiard still yield new surprises, especially through triangle-center loci and conservation laws of 3-periodic orbits that generalize to N-periodic orbits?

source_span.start_text: Can the Elliptic Billiard Still Surprise Us?

sections.summary: The introduction frames the elliptic billiard as an exhaustively studied integrable system and asks whether it can still surprise. It recounts the authors’ earlier discovery that the 3-periodic Incenter locus is an ellipse, the subsequent proofs for several triangle centers, and the experimental approach through an interactive applet and locus gallery. Monge’s Orthoptic Circle is introduced as the bridge to generalizing invariants to N>3.
sections.title: Introduction: Why Revisit the Elliptic Billiard?

source_span.end_text: Let the boundary of the EB satisfy f (x, y) = (x/a)2 + (y/b)2 = 1, where (a, b) are the semi-axes.

sections.summary: Supplies geometric and dynamical background: definitions of triangle centers and derived triangles from Figure 3; the elliptic billiard as a 4D integrable Hamiltonian system with energy and Joachimsthal integrals; Poncelet’s Porism; and Monge’s Orthoptic Circle and its N=4 parallelogram orbits. It sets up vocabulary and classical facts used by the later conservation and locus arguments.
sections.title: Background: Triangle Centers, Integrability, Poncelet, and Monge

source_span.end_text: Every triangle has a circumellipse to which it is a Billiard orbit, whose center coincides with the triangle’s Mittenpunkt.
source_span.start_text: Consider an EB centered at O, and an N = 3 orbit, shown in Figure 6a.

sections.summary: Presents the N=3 locus gallery. Incenter, Barycenter, Circumcenter, Orthocenter, and 9-point center X5 produce ellipses; Excenters produce an ellipse similar to a rotated Incenter locus. Numerically only 29 of the first 100 Kimberling centers yield elliptic loci. Derived triangles generally produce non-elliptic loci, but Extouchpoints form an ellipse identical to the Caustic; Feuerbach Point X11 traces the Caustic while its anticomplement X100 traces the Billiard; Mittenpunkt X9 is stationary at the billiard center, implying every triangle has a Circumbilliard with center at its Mittenpunkt.
sections.title: N=3 Locus Gallery: Ellipses, Exceptions, and the Stationary Mittenpunkt

source_span.end_text: A 3-periodic family conserves the Excentral-to-Orbit area ratio.

sections.summary: Derives the conserved Inradius-to-Circumradius ratio r/R for 3-periodic orbits, expressed as γL−4. Using classical triangle identities, it obtains three conservation corollaries: sum of orbit-angle cosines, product of excentral cosines, and excentral-to-orbit area ratio. It notes r/R is maximal at 0.5 for the circular billiard and tends to zero as a/b→∞.
sections.title: Conserved r/R Ratio and Its Triangle-Identity Corollaries

source_span.start_text: Loci can be ellipses, but can they be a circle?

sections.summary: Begins with the N=3 circular locus of Q1/Q2, centered on the billiard and with radius r*=r(L/4+1/γ), linked to the Excentral Triangle’s Cosine Circle. Then uses N=4/Monge clues to generalize invariants to N>3: stationary tangential-polygon point, generalized extouchpoints on the caustic, conservation of cosine sum and product for all N, odd-N area-ratio conservation, and circular loci for N>4, with a momentum-conservation proof giving radius 1/γ.
sections.title: Circular Loci and Generalizing Invariants to N>3

sections.summary: Concludes with open questions about algebraic/elliptic loci, 3D analogues, self-intersecting orbits, non-billiard Poncelet families, spherical/ellipsoidal billiards, and formulas for remaining constants. It also provides a quick-reference video table and notes a postscript on subsequent proofs for some N>3 invariants.
